query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Al content in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys induces local chemical short‐range ordering that triggers the nucleation of coherent, ordered nanoprecipitates (either B2 or L12 phases) within an FCC matrix. These precipitates govern phase stability by simultaneously impeding dislocation motion, serving as defect sinks (thus enhancing radiation tolerance), stabilizing oxidation behavior, and promoting toughening mechanisms at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A low-Al content alloy (e.g., Al0.1CoCrFeNi) that exhibits a predominantly homogeneous, disordered FCC structure lacking significant ordered precipitate phases.
generation.intervention: Prepare two alloy variants with controlled and rigorously isolated variations in Al content (e.g., Al0.1CoCrFeNi and Al0.3CoCrFeNi) using identical casting, thermomechanical processing, and isothermal annealing conditions (e.g., annealing at 873 K for 24 hours). Additional reference alloys or compositional controls will be incorporated to minimize confounding from other elements.
generation.conditions: All processing parameters (casting, thermomechanical processing, annealing) are kept identical except for the deliberate variation in Al content. Mechanical testing and property evaluation will be performed at room temperature, cryogenic temperatures, and under simulated radiation and oxidation environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The controlled formation and volume fraction of nanoscale, coherent, ordered precipitates (B2 or L12) within the disordered FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Higher Al content increases the atomic size misfit and changes bonding characteristics, driving local chemical short‐range ordering. This ordering nucleates coherent nanoprecipitates that act as barriers to dislocation motion, provide effective sinks for radiation-induced defects, enhance oxidation resistance by stabilizing surface scales, and enable mechanisms such as crack bridging or strain localization that improve toughness at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the low-Al baseline alloy, the high-Al alloy is predicted to develop a dual-phase microstructure characterized by a significant volume fraction of coherent, ordered nanoprecipitates. This microstructural change should correlate with enhanced high-temperature strength, increased resistance to oxidation and radiation damage, and improved cryogenic toughness.
generation.baseline: The low-Al alloy with a homogeneous, disordered FCC structure that exhibits lower high-temperature strength and less resistance to oxidation and radiation, as well as lower toughness at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is tested for Al contents up to around 0.3 moles and under specific annealing conditions (e.g., 873 K for 24 hours). Outside this composition range or processing window, unwanted precipitate formation or embrittlement may occur, violating the hypothesis boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the exact contribution of Al-driven short-range ordering versus other elemental effects. The additional compositional controls are essential to ensure that the observed nanoprecipitate formation is predominantly attributed to changes in Al content.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with systematically varied Al contents (e.g., 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 moles) under identical processing conditions with rigorous compositional control. Characterize the microstructure (using TEM, XRD, etc.) to quantify the volume fraction and coherency of the ordered nanoprecipitates. Evaluate the mechanical properties (high-temperature yield strength, cryogenic toughness), oxidation resistance, and radiation tolerance through standardized tests.
measurements: Quantitative TEM imaging of nanoprecipitate morphology and volume fraction
XRD analysis for phase identification and matrix/precipitate coherency
High-temperature tensile testing to measure yield strength
Oxidation weight gain measurements under high-temperature conditions
Radiation damage simulations or irradiation experiments with defect density analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-Al alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the formation of coherent, ordered nanoprecipitates compared to the low-Al baseline, or if the improvement in mechanical, oxidation, and radiation properties is not observed relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that Al-induced short-range ordering governs phase stability and enhanced properties is falsified.

This composition design aims to ensure that the phase separation can generate a near-equiatomic FCC matrix in situ while forming high-content L12 phases, creating PH-HEAs with superior strength (Fig. 1b). Based on this strategy, we develop a non-equiatomic system Al0.5Cr0.9FeNi2.5V0.2, which has a high Ni concentration of ~50 at% and a high Ni/Al ratio of ~5. Moreover, our alloy excludes Co to reduce the cost and contains ~4 at% V to stabilize and strengthen L12 phases. AbstractStrategies involving metastable phases have been the basis of the design of numerous alloys, yet research on metastable high-entropy alloys is still in its infancy. In dual-phase high-entropy alloys, the combination of local chemical environments and loading-induced crystal structure changes suggests a relationship between deformation mechanisms and chemical atomic distribution, which we examine in here in a Cantor-like Cr20Mn6Fe34Co34Ni6 alloy, comprising both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal closed packed (hcp) phases. We observe that partial dislocation activities result in stable three-dimensional stacking-fault networks. Additionally, the fraction of the stronger hcp phase progressively increases during plastic deformation by forming at the stacking-fault network boundaries in the fcc phase, serving as the major source of strain hardening. The twin boundaries reduce the dislocation mean free path, thus sustaining strain hardening to delay the onset of fracture. This phenomenon is referred to as the “dynamic Hall-Petch” effect (). The increase in yield strength at a lower temperature (77 K) means that critical twinning stress is easily reached because of the relative temperature insensitivity of twinning stress, and thus, nanotwinning occurs at relatively lower strains (). This improves the SHR and delays failure at 77 K, even in the presence of the B2 phase that usually causes strong embrittlement problems at cryogenic temperature. proposals.material_system: AlxCoCrFeNi (with x varied, e.g., comparing Al0.1CoCrFeNi vs. Al0.3CoCrFeNi)
proposals.intervention: Prepare two alloy variants by identical casting and thermomechanical processing followed by isothermal annealing (e.g., 873 K for 24 h) and (optionally) high-strain compression testing
proposals.conditions: Maintain identical processing conditions except for controlled changes in Al content; carry out tests at room temperature, cryogenic temperatures, and under simulated radiation (or oxidation) environments to assess property retention
proposals.structural_mediator: Controlled formation of coherent, ordered L12 (or B2) nanoscale precipitates within a predominantly disordered FCC matrix
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that a critical Al content induces a local chemical short‐range ordering due to the enhanced atomic-size misfit and altered bonding, which triggers the nucleation of ordered nanoprecipitates. These precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion (improving high-temperature strength and radiation defect recombination), stabilize the microstructure against oxidation and phase coarsening, and promote crack-bridging mechanisms that enhance cryogenic toughness. In contrast, lower Al content alloys remain more homogeneous and less capable of forming these beneficial hardening features.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (lower Al content alloy that shows a largely disordered FCC phase), the higher-Al alloy will exhibit a dual-phase microstructure with fine, coherent ordered precipitates. This structural modification is expected to lead to increased high-temperature strength, improved environmental (oxidation) resistance, enhanced radiation tolerance by providing effective defect sinks, and superior cryogenic toughness through refined strain localisation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This mechanistic hypothesis directly links phase stability with the nature and extent of chemical ordering induced by Al content. It creates a controlled comparison that predicts clear changes in microstructural features under specific heat-treatment and deformation conditions. The boundaries are defined by the Al content (up to around 0.3 moles) and the annealing temperature/time regimes, while an absence of ordered precipitate formation under these conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

critiques.addresses_problem: The hypothesis explicitly targets phase stability by linking the increased Al content to local chemical short‐range ordering and subsequent nucleation of ordered nanoprecipitates. This directly addresses the research question by proposing that nanoprecipitate formation governs the desirable properties (high-temperature strength, oxidation resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness) over a controlled comparison between low and high Al alloys.
critiques.constraints: The proposal respects the constraints by working within the AlxCoCrFeNi system and by prescribing identical processing conditions except for controlled Al content variations. It carefully delineates the boundaries (e.g., Al content up to ca. 0.3 moles and specific annealing conditions) to avoid unintended phase formation that could compromise ductility or other properties.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound for this material system. Increased Al content can lead to enhanced atomic-size mismatch and altered bonding, which promotes local chemical ordering and the nucleation of coherent ordered nanoprecipitates (e.g., L12 or B2 phases). These precipitates can serve as barriers to dislocation motion, defect sinks in radiation environments, and enhance crack-bridging at low temperatures, all of which are in line with established metallurgical principles in HEAs.
critiques.feasibility: The experimental approach—including casting, thermomechanical processing, isothermal annealing, and high-strain compression testing—is well within the capabilities of current methods. The controlled variation in Al content and subsequent observations via microstructural characterization are standard practices in alloy research.
critiques.evidence: The supplied records (e.g., PMC8378815, PMC6170471, PMC11396108, PMC7012927) document similar observations regarding the influence of ordered precipitates (whether B2 or L12) on mechanical properties. These works support that a variation in composition (including Al content) can drive nano-scale ordering phenomena that reinforce strength and toughness.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the effect of Al content might be confounded by the influences of other elements or processing conditions, meaning that the observed nanoprecipitate formation might not be solely attributable to the increased Al levels. Additionally, overemphasis on ordered precipitates may lead to embrittlement if not perfectly controlled.
critiques.fix: Incorporate a more rigorous compositional control or additional reference alloys to isolate the effect of Al content, ensuring that contributions from other elements are minimized and that the nanoprecipitate formation mechanism is definitively linked to Al-induced short‐range order.

decision.rationale: We choose direction A because it directly proposes a mechanistic hypothesis linking increased Al content to the formation of coherent ordered nanoprecipitates (e.g., B2 or L12) that stabilize the phase and impart improved mechanical and environmental properties. The critic’s review affirms the physical soundness and relevance of this mechanism but also rightly points out that potential confounding effects from other elements need to be controlled. Therefore, we adopt direction A with the fix of incorporating more rigorous compositional control or additional reference alloys to isolate the effect of Al. This fix preserves the clarity of the hypothesis and ensures that any observed effects can be primarily attributed to variations in Al content.
